title: What Big Data Can and Can't Do
objective: After this level you can explain why huge amounts of data still mislead when they are biased, using Google Flu Trends.
summary: Google Flu Trends read flu from searches, but many matching searches just tracked winter, so it guessed too high for years. Big data should add to careful data, not replace it.

cards.headline: In 2013, Google's flu tracker saw more than double the flu the CDC did.
cards.body: It was built from Google searches, a mountain of data. It still missed, week after week. Why a mountain of data can point the wrong way is this level's lesson.

cards.headline: Reading the flu from searches
cards.body: Google Flu Trends began in 2008 with a simple bet: when flu spreads, flu-related searches rise, so counting searches might track the illness. To build it, engineers sifted about 50 million search terms for the ones whose ups and downs best matched the CDC's flu records. No clinic visits, no lab tests: just the patterns in what people typed.

cards.headline: Part flu detector, part winter detector
cards.body: With 50 million terms to pick from, some matched the flu season by coincidence. Searches about high school basketball, for one, rise with winter, and Google's developers had to weed out terms like that. Researchers who studied the tool called it "part flu detector, part winter detector". It missed the 2009 pandemic, which didn't follow the winter pattern, and from August 2011 it guessed too high in 100 of 108 weeks. By February 2013 its estimate of flu doctor visits was more than double the CDC's.

cards.fact: Big data works best as a supplement, not a substitute.
cards.context: The researchers named the mistake "big data hubris": assuming a giant new data set can replace traditional data collection instead of adding to it. When they combined Google's numbers with the CDC's delayed reports, the mix beat either one alone. In 2015 Google stopped publishing its own flu estimates and shared its data with researchers, including the CDC. More data isn't better data if it measures the wrong thing.

questions.prompt: Put Google Flu Trends' story in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Stopped publishing its own flu estimates
questions.explanation: Google Flu Trends began in 2008, missed the 2009 pandemic, and by February 2013 was more than double the CDC's estimate. In 2015 Google stopped publishing its own flu estimates.

questions.prompt: A city plans to scrap its road traffic counters and estimate traffic from social media posts alone. What would the Google Flu researchers warn?

options.label: More posts will always cancel out the errors
options.rationale: Google had 50 million terms and still guessed too high for years.

options.label: Social media data are too small to be useful
options.rationale: The problem wasn't size; it was what the data measured.

options.label: Traffic can never be measured reliably
options.rationale: It can: that's what the counters already do.

options.label: Use the posts to add to the counters, not replace them

questions.explanation: That is "big data hubris": treating new data as a substitute instead of a supplement. Google plus the CDC beat either alone.

questions.prompt: In February 2013, Google's flu estimate was more than double the CDC's. As a percent change, it was too high by more than what?

options.rationale: Doubling adds the whole starting amount, not a sliver.
Half as much again would be 1.5 times, not double.
That would be triple, not double.

questions.explanation: Double means the extra equals the starting value: change ÷ start = 1, or 100%, just as $50 back to $100 is a 100% rise.
